results.content: Google Japan has a new keyboard out, and this time you don't go hunting for the keys because they come to you. The Gboard Kurukuru Version puts its keys on four little conveyor belts that keep rolling, and you simply tap the letter you want when it slides under your finger.There are 29 keys on each belt, so 116 in all. Capital and small letters get their own keys too, which means you never have to touch Shift.If you're worried about timing your taps, a voice calls out each key as it reaches a set point. Feeling confident? There's a speed mode that spins the belts faster. And if you miss your letter, well, you wait for it to come back around.It plays a lot like a rhythm game.The idea, Google says, is to make one-handed typing easier. On a normal keyboard your hand has to move around to [...] On a normal keyboard your hand has to move around to find the keys, and that gets tiring fast with one hand, let alone one finger. Here the keys do the moving, so your other hand is free for the mouse or, as Google puts it, a cup of tea.The company even calls it a "Copernican revolution" in typing, and says you can build a second one if you want to type with both hands. "Kurukuru" loosely means spinning round and round in Japanese, which pretty much sums it up. [...] As you'd expect, there's no buy option for this one. Google has instead put the whole design up on GitHub as an open-source project, so if you've got the parts and the patience, you can build one at home.This is the 15th keyboard Google Japan has dreamt up for October 1, a tradition that took over from its April Fools' jokes in 2021. The date is a little joke of its own, since 10/1 reads as 101, as in the old 101-key keyboard.Before this, we got the extra-long Gboard Bar, the wearable Gboard Caps and last year's Gboard Dial, which had you typing like you were dialling a rotary phone. Google says faster belts, longer and portable versions, and more colours could be next, so the wait for your next letter might get a bit shorter.

# Google Unveils A Physical Gboard On Conveyor Belts

By Paulo Montenegro, on 10/09/2026 07:50 PDT

Google Japan has introduced its latest experimental hardware interface, the Gboard Kurukuru Version, a concept peripheral that reverses standard typing mechanics by placing individual keys on motorized conveyor belts. Rather than requiring hands to travel across a static surface, the device continuously transports characters directly to the user’s fingertips. [...] The hardware architecture relies on four continuous belts, each carrying 29 switches for a total of 116 keys. As the mechanical tracks rotate, the user keeps their hand relatively stationary, timing input execution as the targeted letter rolls into position. The design supports direct entry of both uppercase and lowercase characters and enables complete navigation using only one hand or a single finger.

This operational layout frees the secondary hand for external desktop tasks, such as navigating a mouse or holding a drink. The Kurukuru marks the 15th iteration in Google Japan’s ongoing series of unconventional input experiments, following earlier releases such as a single elongated linear row, a double-sided loop, and rotary telephone dials. Google Japan has looked at the conventional keyboard and decided that perhaps our fingers have been doing too much of the work. Developed by the Gboard team, the new Gboard Kurukuru Version places its keys on moving conveyor belts, allowing characters to travel toward the user rather than asking the user to reach across a fixed layout. The experimental device turns one of the most familiar tools on a desk into something closer to a miniature production line, with typing becoming a matter of catching the right character as it rolls into place. [...] Kurukuru arrives as the 15th entry in Google Japan’s long-running series of unconventional Gboard experiments. Previous editions have stretched the keyboard into a single elongated row, twisted it into a double-sided loop and, in 2025, replaced traditional typing with rotary telephone-style dials. The latest version continues that habit of taking an everyday interface far too literally, then engineering it seriously enough to work. Google is also considering color variations, a high-speed mode and longer or more portable short versions, although none have been announced as commercial products.

# Google Japan Put Keyboard Keys on Four Moving Conveyor Belts

RP

By Rei Padla  · 4 min read

  Google Keyboard Gboard Kurukuru 

If you buy something from a link in this article, we may earn a commission. Learn more

Most keyboard innovation promises faster typing, greater comfort, or less hand movement. Google Japan’s latest Gboard concept takes that last idea literally: instead of making you reach for the keys, it brings them toward your fingers on four looping conveyor belts.

Called the Gboard “Kurukuru” version, this is not a new feature for the Gboard app on your phone. It is a physical DIY keyboard concept announced on October 1, 2026, with open-source designs rather than a retail price or purchase link. [...] Google also floats a possible high-speed mode, along with longer and shorter versions. These are ideas mentioned in the announcement, not confirmed features of a forthcoming retail device.

Neither the announcement nor the build guide provides usability testing that establishes improvements in comfort, accessibility, typing speed, or accuracy. For now, Kurukuru is an unusual interaction experiment, not a proven ergonomic solution.

That distinction matters. Moving the keys instead of your hands is an intriguing design choice, but it does not automatically make typing easier.

## Open source, not on sale

Google says it has no plans to sell Kurukuru. Instead, it has released designs so people can build a similar device themselves. [...] The build guide includes 3D-print files, a parts list, mechanical assembly steps, and firmware resources. Its moving-key version uses 116 low-profile switches and keycaps, a geared motor, a motor driver, and an ATOMS3 Lite controller. This is a substantial assembly project, not a keyboard kit you simply plug in.

There is also an important limitation: the guide lists electronics and wiring documentation as “coming soon.” It separately identifies a functional Bluetooth keyboard edition that is also still forthcoming. The available instructions should therefore not be mistaken for a finished guide to a fully functional wireless keyboard.
